title: A Sultan of Many Tongues
subtitle: How a Learned Bahmani Sultan Carved Empire with Sword, Treaty and Tongue
region: Gulbarga, Raichur Doab and Vijayanagara frontier
moral: A ruler who listens in many languages hears more of his people.

sources.note: Main narrative for Firuz Shah's accession, campaigns, multilingualism and court.

sources.citation: Dakhni verses attributed to Firuz Shah in later anthologies
sources.note: Evidence for the tradition of early royal Dakhni authorship, though individual attributions are debated.

sources.citation: Vijayanagara copper-plate evidence for frontier-war chronology
sources.note: Corroborates the wider setting of Bahmani-Vijayanagara conflict.

sources.citation: Tariq Rahman, From Hindi to Urdu, OUP, 2011
sources.note: Places Dakhni in the long history of Urdu and Deccan literary culture.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of a throne hall fading into a battlefield and a script-covered sky

dialogue.text: In the dusty Deccan between Gulbarga and Raichur, Sultan Firuz Shah Bahmani fought Vijayanagara by steel and treaty, and let many tongues—Persian and Dakhni, Kannada and Telugu—speak in his court.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a tense palace corridor at night

dialogue.text: In 1397, the Bahmani palace at Gulbarga hissed with plots. When the old Sultan died, Ferishta says, rival princes and nobles moved in the corridors by torchlight, each weighing the throne in his own mind.

panels.shot: medium close-up profile of Firuz listening to two factions arguing in the shadows

dialogue.text: Ferishta records a palace struggle. Firuz, son of Daud Khan and nephew of the first Bahmani, watched factions harden around other claimants, and knew that hesitation could cost his life.

panels.shot: epic hall wide as Firuz steps toward the throne with armed supporters behind

dialogue.text: The chronicles say he moved first. Backed by loyal amirs and soldiers, Firuz seized the palace, checked his rivals, and was proclaimed Sultan Taj ud-Din Firuz Shah Bahmani in Gulbarga.

panels.shot: low-angle medium on Firuz seated on the throne with books and weapons flanking him

dialogue.text: Unlike many warlords, Firuz had trained his mind as much as his arm. Ferishta praises him as a learned Sultan, and later scholars judge it plausible that he knew Arabic, Persian and Turkish, and learned the tongues of the Deccan.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder view of Firuz speaking with two officials in different regional garb

dialogue.speaker: taj_ud_din_firuz_shah_bahmani
dialogue.text: To hold this land, we must hear every tongue it speaks.

panels.shot: bird's-eye wide of the Deccan with Raichur Doab highlighted between two rivers

dialogue.text: Between the Krishna and Tungabhadra lay the Raichur Doab, rich in grain and taxes, key to war-horses from the west. Both Bahmani and Vijayanagara kings fought for it, year after year.

panels.shot: dynamic battlefield wide of Bahmani army advancing toward Raichur fort

dialogue.text: Ferishta describes Firuz leading repeated campaigns toward Raichur. Vijayanagara copper-plates confirm that on this frontier, in these years, Deccan and Kannada kings clashed in long, costly wars.

panels.shot: close-up of Firuz on horseback surveying a smoking battlefield from a distance

dialogue.text: Ferishta tells of desperate assaults and heavy losses, and gives vast casualty figures that historians now treat with caution. Whatever the exact numbers, the wars for Raichur bled men, money and grain on both sides.

panels.shot: medium wide inside a Bahmani war council tent with maps and horse traders depicted

dialogue.text: These were not only battles of creed. Ferishta notes disputes over territory and tribute, and the horse trade from the Arabian Sea. Control of the Doab meant feeding armies and buying cavalry from overseas.

panels.shot: tense frontal shot of Firuz and a Vijayanagara envoy facing each other in a pavilion

dialogue.speaker: taj_ud_din_firuz_shah_bahmani
dialogue.text: We can count dead men, or we can count seasons of peace.

panels.shot: symbolic split-panel style wide of a marriage procession and a frontier fort

dialogue.text: After a hard-won victory over Vijayanagara, Ferishta mentions marriage ties sealing the peace. Modern historians read these as diplomatic alliances, binding frontier politics with family and dowry.

panels.shot: court wide of Gulbarga durbar with Hindus and Muslims standing together in official dress

dialogue.text: Ferishta notes that Firuz widened the circle of service. He brought more Hindu officers into his administration, tying local knowledge and loyalties to the Bahmani state, even as he rewarded his old Deccan companions.

panels.shot: medium shot of Firuz listening to a Dakhni-speaking petitioner in simple clothes

dialogue.text: Here, the language of power began to bend. Persian stayed the idiom of farmans and high poetry, but in the audience hall, Dakhni—the north Indian speech formed in the Deccan—grew louder beside it.

panels.shot: intimate interior medium of Firuz writing by lamplight with multiple scripts around him

dialogue.text: Later anthologies preserve Dakhni verses in his name. Scholars debate which lines are truly his, yet the very tradition remembers Firuz as a Sultan who not only ruled, but also wrote in the Deccan’s own speech.

panels.shot: visual metaphor wide of words flowing from palace into streets in different scripts

dialogue.text: Tariq Rahman and others place this Dakhni in the long story of Urdu. In the Deccan, under rulers like Firuz, a courtly, mixed speech slowly took shape, hearing both northern idioms and southern tongues.

panels.shot: medium close-up of an older Firuz, thoughtful, with maps and books behind

dialogue.speaker: taj_ud_din_firuz_shah_bahmani
dialogue.text: Steel yields to rust. Words cross mountains.

panels.shot: somber interior wide of Firuz’s bier surrounded by nobles of many communities

dialogue.text: Firuz Shah died in 1422, leaving a kingdom that would soon fracture. Yet in Ferishta’s pages and in Dakhni lines ascribed to him, he remains a ruler remembered for both campaigns and conversations.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide of Gulbarga and Bidar skylines dissolving into modern Deccan cities

dialogue.text: On the Bahmani frontier, Firuz Shah learned to wield languages like tools of state. His Deccan reminds us that when power listens in many tongues, it hears more of the land it claims.
